\chapter{An Adult Swimming Course}
\label{ch:curso-nadar-adulto}
\hlchaptermodality{417}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can understand a simple notice for an adult swimming course.}

Retrieve course, swim, and adult in a short class notice.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el curso]{el curso — a path of learning}

\label{lesson:ES-C417-curso}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{aprender}, to learn. A planned path for learning something is \textbf{un curso}, a course or class.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{cursus} meant a running or a course, from \textbf{currere}, to run. English \textbf{course} keeps the same idea of a route, while \textbf{current} is something running onward. A learning course is a route followed from lesson to lesson.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: name the subject}]
The noun is masculine: \textbf{el curso}, \textbf{un curso}. Use \textbf{de} to name its subject: \textbf{un curso de natación}, a swimming course.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el curso}
  \item \emph{un curso}
  \item \emph{un curso de natación}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Course? (\emph{El curso}.) A swimming course? (\emph{Un curso de natación}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/curso}{DLE: curso}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nadar]{nadar — move through the water}

\label{lesson:ES-C417-nadar}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{la piscina} and \textbf{un curso}. What might a course at a pool teach? \textbf{Nadar}, to swim.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Spanish \textbf{nadar} continues Latin \textbf{natāre}, to swim. English keeps the root in \textbf{natatorium}, a building with a swimming pool. The infinitive ends in \textbf{-ar}, like many familiar action words.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: learn to swim}]
After \textbf{aprender}, Spanish uses \textbf{a} before another verb: \textbf{aprender a nadar}, to learn to swim. The related noun is \textbf{la natación}, swimming, as in \textbf{curso de natación}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nadar}
  \item \emph{aprender a nadar}
  \item \emph{un curso de natación}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To swim? (\emph{Nadar}.) To learn to swim? (\emph{Aprender a nadar}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/nadar}{DLE: nadar}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[adulto, adulta]{adulto, adulta — fully grown}

\label{lesson:ES-C417-adulto}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{un curso} and \textbf{nadar}. If this class is for grown-ups, the notice says \textbf{para adultos}, for adults.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{adultus} meant grown up, from \textbf{adolescere}, to grow. English \textbf{adult} is the same word with its ending shortened. Spanish keeps the ending and matches gender and number: \textbf{adulto}, \textbf{adulta}, \textbf{adultos}, \textbf{adultas}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: say who it is for}]
Use \textbf{para} for the intended group: \textbf{un curso de natación para adultos}. The plural \textbf{adultos} can describe a mixed group or a group of men.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{adulto, adulta}
  \item \emph{para adultos}
  \item \emph{un curso de natación para adultos}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Adult? (\emph{Adulto, adulta}.) For adults? (\emph{Para adultos}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/adulto}{DLE: adulto}.
\end{tcolorbox}
